en: Jātaka:
Miscellaneous Section,
Chapter on the Rice Field of Śālī Rice.
3. The Mahāukkusajātaka “Criminals are binding torches to light the island;
they long to devour me.”
"Tell me, Senaka, of a friend and a companion;
speak of the calamity that befell the kinsmen of the birds.
"You are the most excellent among the birds, O winged one! said the bird to the birds.
O King Ukkusa, we go to you for refuge;
my subjects desire to devour me, so may you,
O fierce Cīla, be for my happiness.
“Wise people make friends and companions,
seeking happiness at the right time and the wrong time.
Senaka, I shall explain this matter to you.”
For the Noble One performs what is the duty of the Noble One.
Whatever duty must be done by one who is compassionate,
that has been performed for you here by the Noble One through his nobility.
“Protect yourself and do not grieve;
we shall obtain sons while you are still alive.
“While providing protection and shelter for you alone,” he said.
"Even when my body is broken, I shall not tremble;
some friends perform services for their friends,
even giving up their own lives— this is the way of the virtuous."
“The kurara bird performed a difficult task for the sake of its offspring,
O egg-born one.”
“Even when the middle of the night has not yet come,
some who have fallen away through their own actions are established again out of compassion for their friends.”
"My sons are mine; I have come to you for refuge.
You two should act for my benefit, O water-dwellers.
"With wealth, with grain, and even with our own selves..."
The wise make friends and companions; I shall do this for you,
Senaka, for a noble person performs what is required for another noble person.
“Be free from anxiety, dear father, and sit down;
the son performs service for the benefit of his father.
I shall perform this service for you.”
“Protecting the sons of Sena.
“Truly, dear father, this is the way of the righteous:
that a son should act for the welfare of his father.”
“May the sons of Sena, upon seeing me with my body fully grown, not harm me. “O best of those who live by hunting deer,
humans treat cattle as food.”
Those overcome by fear go forth to the highest state;
my sons, driven by possessiveness, have come to this destination. You are our king; be for our happiness.
“I shall accomplish this purpose for you, Senaka;
I am coming to see you for your destruction.
For how could a wise man, capable and fully conscious, [act otherwise]?”
Nor indeed is this for the protection of one's own kin.
One should make friends who are kind-hearted,
and one should make them noble for the sake of attaining happiness.
Having spread out a rug as if it were a garment,
we rejoice, being united with our children,
through the deed of our own friend.
The hairy birds, heart-stealing and warbling, warble in response to their companion who does not flee.
Having obtained a friend as a companion,
the wise man enjoys his children, cattle, or wealth,
thinking: "I, my children, and my husband are mine."
Possessing compassion for friends,
these things— wealth and heroism— belong to one who has a good companion, just as they do to a king.
Thus, one who possesses friends, who is renowned,
and whose spirit is exalted, enjoys himself in this world as he desires.
One should cultivate friendships.
Even though he was struck down by Dalidda, Senaka,
behold how out of compassion for his friend,
he brought his kinsmen together in harmony.
The wise man who, being strong and courageous, makes friends—
thus he becomes happy.
"Just as I am, so are you and Senaka," he said.
This concludes the third Jātaka, the Mahāukkusajātaka.
